questions.question: Q: What percentage of the GCSE is the Depth Study worth?
questions.correctAnswer: 50% — it is Paper 2, equally weighted with the Period Study (Paper 1).

questions.question: Q: What is the key difference between the Period Study and the Depth Study?
questions.correctAnswer: The Period Study covers a broad period focusing on narrative and causation; the Depth Study covers a shorter period in detail, emphasising source analysis and interpretations.

questions.question: Q: Why must you combine source evidence with your own knowledge?
questions.correctAnswer: Because your own contextual knowledge allows you to evaluate the source's accuracy, identify what it omits, and provide a fuller analysis than the source alone can give.

tests.name: Exam-Style Practice
tests.description: Short-answer practice on Depth Study Technique

questions.question: Q: What should you consider when explaining why two interpretations differ?
questions.correctAnswer: The evidence each historian used, their perspective or school of thought, what they chose to emphasise or omit, and when the interpretation was written.

questions.question: Q: How should you refer to sources in your answer?
questions.correctAnswer: By name or provenance (e.g., 'Herodotus states...' or 'The Athenian inscription records...'), not just 'the source says'.

questions.question: Full-Mark Response How far do the sources support the view that Pericles was the most important Athenian politician of the 5th century BCE? (15 marks) <div class="
questions.correctAnswer: The sources largely support the view that Pericles was the most important Athenian politician, though they also reveal limitations to his influence. Thucydides provides the strongest support, describing Pericles as 'the first citizen of Athens' who led the people rather than being led by them. His account of Pericles' Funeral Oration shows a leader who defined Athenian identity and values. Plutarch, writing later, reinforces this view by devoting an entire biography to Pericles, emphasising his political dominance, his building programme on the Acropolis, and his management of the Delian League. The archaeological evidence of the Parthenon and other Periclean buildings physically demonstrates his ability to direct Athenian resources on an unprecedented scale. However, the sources also reveal counter-arguments. Thucydides himself notes that Pericles was temporarily deposed and fined after the Spartan invasion of Attica, showing his influence had limits. Aristophanes' comedies mock Pericles and his associates, reminding us that he faced significant political opposition. The death of Pericles in 429 BCE from the plague did not end Athenian democracy or the Peloponnesian War, suggesting the institutions he worked within had their own momentum. Furthermore, other politicians like Cimon and Cleon were also significant — Cimon built the Delian League's power before Pericles, and Cleon continued the war effort after.
